Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

A rainy street in 1877, read for depth

Describe

Gustave Caillebotte painted Paris in 1877: umbrellas, top hats, a long coat, wet paving stones. Say what is near and what is far.

Cues

Which clues tell you? Look at the shrinking stones, the overlapping bodies and the size of the distant walkers.

Critical

The couple's clothes look solid and heavy. What does the painting not tell you about how those clothes fit?

Image: Caillebotte’s 1877 painting of a Paris street in the rain: fashionable walkers under umbrellas, paving stones shrinking toward the distance.

Gustave Caillebotte - Paris Street; Rainy Day - Google Art Project · Gustave Caillebotte · Public domain · Source

  • Model the first block aloud; pairs do the rest.
  • Keep the answers: they return in the cue ledger.

Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

One silhouette, several honest volumes

Rei Kawakubo builds garments that do not follow the body's outline. From one view, the eye cannot tell padding from body: the silhouette alone does not decide the volume.

Photographed in the 2017 Kawakubo exhibition at the Met, New York. Which second view would settle the question?

Image: Dresses by Rei Kawakubo - Sarah Stierch 01.jpg

Dresses by Rei Kawakubo - Sarah Stierch 01 · Sarah Stierch (photograph); Rei Kawakubo (garments) · CC BY 4.0 · Source

  • The paradox of the whole lecture: a flat outline fits many volumes.
  • Ask for the cheapest second view: side, back, or movement?

Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

Seeing solves an inverse problem

Many different scenes can send the same image to the eye. Seeing depth means choosing one of them — and the choice can be wrong.

In an Ames room, a slanted room seen through a peephole looks square, so two people of the same height look like a giant and a child.

Image: Diagram of an Ames room: a trapezoidal room seen through a peephole looks rectangular, so two people at different distances appear giant and tiny.

Ames room · Alex valavanis · Public domain · Source

  • Adelbert Ames Jr. built the room in 1946.
  • The eye prefers 'square room' over 'equal people': a learned bet.

One picture, many worlds

  • Point to the three objects: same image, three worlds.
  • This is why a fashion still needs a second view.

Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

The brain bets that light comes from above

In the 1860s Hermann von Helmholtz called seeing unconscious inference: a fast guess from experience. Turn this lunar crater upside down and the hollow becomes a dome.

Your folds obey the same bet: light a pleat from below and it can turn inside out.

Image: Two lunar orbiter photographs of the same crater; rotated 180 degrees, the hollow crater reads as a raised dome.

Crater illusion · NASA / GSFC / Arizona State University · Public domain · Source

  • Rotate a phone photo of a quilted jacket: the quilting flips too.
  • Helmholtz: Handbook of Physiological Optics, vol. 3 (1867).

Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

Depth as something you can fall into

In 1960 Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk placed babies on glass over a drop. Most would not crawl across the visual cliff: they read depth as danger, not as theory.

James J. Gibson argued that a moving viewer picks up depth directly from texture, flow and horizon in the light.

Image: Infant on a glass visual cliff apparatus used in Gibson and Walk depth-perception research

NIH visual cliff experiment (cropped) · Gibson and Walk (1960) via NIH / Nature Publishing Group · CC BY 4.0 · Source · cropped

  • Gibson (1979): the ecological approach; motion parallax and optic flow.
  • Studio translation: walk around the garment before you trust one photo.

Three ways to explain seeing depth

  • Frames, not dogma: each one gives a different studio test.
  • Marr's 2½-D sketch returns in lecture C.

Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

Seven clues a flat picture can give

Occlusion, relative size, perspective, texture, haze, shading and motion parallax let a flat image suggest depth. Each one is a clue, not proof.

Image: Diagram plate of pictorial depth cues including occlusion, size, and perspective

Depth cues 1 · Brazzit · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Source

  • Ask pairs to find four of the seven in the Caillebotte painting.
  • Binocular cues (two eyes) are what a flat picture cannot give.

What a cue proves — and what it cannot

Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

Pictorial revolutions start in perception

The cognitive scientist Margaret Boden argues that Renaissance perspective and Cubism were both creative because they worked on how the mind turns flat images into scenes.

the set of psychological processes that make it possible for the mind to interpret two-dimensional images as depicting three-dimensional scenes

(Boden 2004, 23)

An image is creative when it changes what a viewer infers, not when it adds more detail.

Image: Black-and-white 1912 book plate of a crowded Venetian Adoration of the Magi: figures in rich garments stacked up the picture rather than receding to one vanishing point.

The Venetian School of Painting (1912) · Internet Archive Book Images · PD · Source

  • Boden 2004, 22–23: perspective and Cubism grounded in the same 2D→3D processes.
  • Point at the plate: depth by stacking, before one measured box.

Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

Recall check

Alone, from memory, three minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. Why can one flat image fit many 3D scenes?
  2. What did Helmholtz call seeing?
  3. What did babies do at the visual cliff?
  4. Name three pictorial depth cues.
  5. Which depth cue can prove how a garment fits?

Course geometric background · threshold · #c378606cc29b · Original course SVG

Answers:

  • The eye receives a 2D projection: the inverse problem.
  • Unconscious inference.
  • Most refused to crawl over the drop.
  • Any three of occlusion, size, perspective, texture, haze, shading, motion parallax.
  • None: a cue is evidence about the picture, not the body.

Exercise 1 · Cue audit

Volume and depth · Lecture A of 3

Exercise 2 · Flip the light

Light the same folds twice with a phone torch: once from above, once from below. Find the frame where a hollow reads as a bump.

Set-up in the lesson

Keep both frames and one sentence: which bet did your eye make, and which view would correct it?

Image: A long black finely pleated silk Delphos gown on a mannequin.

Museo del Traje - MT111885 - Vestido Delphos · Museo del Traje (photograph); Mariano Fortuny y Madrazo (gown) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Source

  • Pleated or quilted fabric works best; dark room, torch at 45°.
  • No AI needed today.
